issues.subcategory: contradictory operationalization of moral incongruence
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly defines moral incongruence as the interaction between moral disapproval and behavioral frequency, but later states that it will be measured as the interaction between moral disapproval and severity of consequences. These are conceptually and statistically different predictors. If severity consequences are used in the interaction, the model becomes partially tautological because consequences overlap with the outcome/problem severity. This inconsistency undermines the preregistered hypothesis and makes replication and interpretation ambiguous.
issues.quote: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action. That is, the present study seeks to test whether the observed effects of interactions present in prior literature for pornography use (i.e., between moral disapproval and frequency of use) extend to addictive disorders more broadly.

issues.subcategory: SESOI value inconsistency
issues.description: The analytic plan says the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test will use an equivalence region based on SESOI δ = .27, but the next paragraph says the equivalence region is δ = |.11|. These are very different equivalence bounds and would lead to different conclusions. This is a critical preregistration ambiguity because the key confirmatory claims depend on equivalence testing.
issues.quote: We will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression (Counsell & Cribbie, 2015), with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27.

issues.subcategory: conflicting equivalence interval
issues.description: The manuscript explicitly describes the primary equivalence region as both .27 and .11. The later rationale describes .11 as 'extremely conservative,' but this conflicts with the earlier stated δ = .27 and with later fallback plans using .23. Without a single fixed equivalence bound, the registered report leaves substantial discretion after seeing data.
issues.quote: Collectively, then, setting our equivalence region to δ= |.11| represents an extremely conservative analytic decision.

issues.subcategory: post hoc redefinition of equivalence region
issues.description: The plan proposes changing the equivalence interval after observing whether non-pornography effects exceed the primary SESOI. This creates a data-dependent inferential rule that can preserve the preferred conclusion by switching from testing practical nullness to testing whether effects are smaller than the pornography effect. Such contingent analysis inflates interpretive flexibility and weakens confirmatory claims.
issues.quote: In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects of moral incongruence for gambling and substances exceed our region of equivalence based on our SESOI, we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.

issues.subcategory: contingent underpowered subgroup analysis plan
issues.description: For low-prevalence substances, the authors plan to change the equivalence region if they lack power to test the originally specified equivalence hypothesis. This converts an inability to establish equivalence to a different, less stringent comparison. The decision criteria for 'lack power' are not fully specified and allow selective reinterpretation of null or inconclusive findings.
issues.quote: Should we lack power to sufficient test equivalence with null effects for the above behaviors, we will adjust analyses accordingly. Specifically, rather than testing whether or not the effect of moral incongruence for these behaviors falls within the region of equivalence for our primary SESOI, we will test an alternative model where our equivalence region is defined by the lower bound of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate of moral incongruence in predicting self-reported addiction to pornography

issues.subcategory: incorrect or inconsistent conversion among effect sizes
issues.description: The manuscript reports several conversions among ΔR2, f2, Cohen's d, and β without sufficient justification and with apparent inconsistencies. For example, ΔR2 = .012 corresponds approximately to f2 = .012 if based only on incremental R2 over a near-zero base, not .016 necessarily; converting a regression interaction f2 to Cohen's d requires assumptions that are not stated. These conversions are used to justify equivalence bounds, so errors or unjustified transformations affect the main inferential framework.
issues.quote: Prior studies of moral incongruence have found moral incongruence to have small (ΔR2 = .014, f2 = .020, Cohen’s d = .24, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020; ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen’s d = .22, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020), to moderate (ΔR2 = .072,  f2 = .12, Cohen’s d = .69; Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020), to relatively large (ΔR2 = .12, f2 = .23, Cohen’s d = .97, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020) effects

issues.subcategory: power analysis mismatch for equivalence testing
issues.description: The power analysis appears based on detecting a nonzero regression effect at α = .05, not on power for equivalence testing using the specified Anderson-Hauck procedure and equivalence bounds. Power to reject a null of non-equivalence is not the same as power to detect f2 = .015. Therefore, the conclusion that the study is adequately powered for equivalence is not established.
issues.quote: using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2009), we conducted a power analysis to determine the sample size needed to reliably detect our smallest effect of interest (f2 = .015), a series of sensitivity analyses to determine the likely power our final sample sizes would have to detect the effect size associated with our SESOI and equivalence region defined above

issues.subcategory: not accounting for complex sampling and oversampling
issues.description: The total sample combines a nationally matched sample and a sports-wagering oversample, but the analytic plan does not specify sampling weights, stratification variables, or procedures to obtain population-representative estimates. Treating the combined sample as a simple random U.S. sample will overrepresent gamblers and likely distort estimates and standard errors, especially for gambling and correlates related to sports wagering.
issues.quote: the target sample size will be 2,500 American adults that match nationally representative norms for age and gender. Furthermore... we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically. This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.subcategory: representativeness overclaim
issues.description: The manuscript describes the study as nationally representative despite matching only on age and gender and then adding a large nonrepresentative sports-wagering oversample. Without weighting and more complete demographic calibration, the combined sample is not representative of the U.S. population. Claims about the American public and population-level addiction processes are therefore overextended.
issues.quote: This work will make use of an upcoming study (N=4,000) involving a representative sample of the U.S. population (n=2,500) and a sample of sports-wagering individuals in the U.S. (n=1,500).

issues.subcategory: missing weighting and survey design details
issues.description: The methods do not report whether YouGov will provide sampling weights, which benchmark variables will be used, whether the sports-wagering oversample will be weighted into or excluded from population analyses, or how variance estimation will reflect panel matching. These details are necessary to evaluate inferential validity and reproducibility.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms.

issues.subcategory: online panel quality control not specified
issues.description: The manuscript relies on YouGov proprietary quality procedures and states that no exclusions are anticipated, but does not describe attention checks, duplicate prevention, speeding criteria, straight-lining checks, bot detection, or how panel data quality will be audited. Proprietary assurances are insufficient for replication and evaluation of data validity.
issues.quote: certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards. Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding.

issues.subcategory: unjustified assumption of no missing data
issues.description: The authors anticipate no unplanned missingness but do not specify how missingness, item nonresponse, breakoffs, 'prefer not to answer,' panel-data missingness, or invalid skip-pattern responses will be handled. Sensitive topics such as pornography, illicit drug use, and gambling commonly produce missing or nonresponse data, and omission of a plan may bias estimates.
issues.quote: Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.subcategory: single-item moral disapproval measures
issues.description: Moral disapproval is central to the hypotheses but is measured with a single item for each behavior. Single items cannot assess reliability, dimensionality, or distinctions among moral wrongness, legal disapproval, health concerns, religious concerns, stigma, and perceived harm. Measurement error and construct underrepresentation may attenuate or distort interactions across domains.
issues.quote: Additionally, we will include a series of single-item moral disapproval questions that match previous measures of moral disapproval of pornography. For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement “I believe that using ________ is morally wrong”

issues.subcategory: nonparallel moral-disapproval content across substances
issues.description: The moral disapproval items are not conceptually parallel across behaviors. For prescription drugs the item specifies non-medical reasons, for illicit drugs it invokes illegality, and for cannabis wording varies with legality. Moral wrongness may reflect legal status, public-health risk, or nonmedical misuse rather than moral incongruence. This threatens cross-domain comparisons and the claim of uniqueness to pornography.
issues.quote: I believe that using prescription drugs for non-medical reasons is morally wrong... I believe that using illegal/illicit drugs is morally wrong.

issues.subcategory: ASSIST modified beyond validation
issues.description: The study modifies the ASSIST substantially: response categories are changed, behaviors such as pornography and gambling are added, only selected items are averaged, and scoring departs from validated risk-score procedures. These changes may invalidate comparisons with substance-use disorder symptoms and make the resulting 'problematic use' score psychometrically uncertain.
issues.quote: To assess substance use behaviors, we will use a modified version of the Alcohol, Smoking and Substance Involvement Screening Test... We will also include pornography and gambling as response options on the NIDA-ASSIST... Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography

issues.subcategory: averaging non-equivalent ASSIST item scales
issues.description: The proposed outcome averages items with different time frames and scale ranges: three frequency items scored 0–5 for past three months and two lifetime/past-three-month items scored 0, 3, 6. Averaging these assumes equal intervals and equal construct loadings despite different response formats and temporal references. This can distort severity scores and interactions.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to three frequency based questions... on a scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day)... Participants will also respond to two questions... on 3 point scale (0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months). Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged

issues.subcategory: outcome contamination by moral guilt
issues.description: The Brief Pornography Screen includes guilt about pornography use, and the PGSI includes guilt about gambling. Because moral disapproval is a predictor, including guilt/moralized distress in the outcome can inflate associations and interactions between moral disapproval and 'addiction' symptoms. This threatens the interpretation that effects reflect perceived addiction rather than overlap between moral distress and outcome items.
issues.quote: 5. You continue to use pornography even though you feel guilty about it.

issues.subcategory: outcome contamination by gambling guilt item
issues.description: The gambling outcome includes an item about guilt, which is closely related to moral disapproval and moral incongruence. This creates criterion contamination and may make gambling appear more morally influenced or, depending on scoring, confound moral distress with gambling severity.
issues.quote: Have you felt guilty about the way you gamble or what happens when you gamble?

issues.subcategory: BPS response scale conflict
issues.description: The main text states that the Brief Pornography Screen uses a 0–2 response scale, but the supplemental materials show 0, 2, and 4. This affects total scores and comparability with validated scoring/cutoffs, and it is unclear which scoring will be used.
issues.quote: Participants will respond... on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed.

issues.subcategory: PGSI response scale conflict
issues.description: The main text states the PGSI uses a 0–3 scale, but the supplemental table lists response values 0, 2, 4, and 5. This is inconsistent with standard PGSI scoring and with the manuscript’s description. The scoring choice will affect severity distributions and model estimates.
issues.quote: This 9-item measure requires participants to respond... on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged.

issues.subcategory: frequency scale coding conflict
issues.description: The methods describe pornography frequency as a 1–6 scale, but the supplemental measure uses 0–5. Similar discrepancies occur for ASSIST frequency. Centering and regression estimates depend on coding, so the preregistered analysis is ambiguous.
issues.quote: Pornography viewing frequency will be assessed... on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day).

issues.subcategory: number of target behaviors inconsistent
issues.description: The analytic plan states there are eight proposed outcomes and eight moderation analyses, but the listed target behaviors appear to be seven domains, with pornography and gambling each sometimes having two outcomes. Table 1 lists seven target behavior/substance rows, while the text says eight target behaviors/variables. The multiplicity and confirmatory hypothesis structure are unclear.
issues.quote: Prior to our primary analyses, assumptions of regression... will be tested for each of the eight proposed outcomes.

issues.subcategory: Table 1 omits nicotine split described in measures
issues.description: The modified ASSIST scoring text refers to separate tobacco and non-tobacco nicotine outcomes, but Table 1 collapses tobacco/nicotine products. This creates uncertainty about whether tobacco and nicotine are analyzed separately or jointly, affecting the number of models and measurement interpretation.
issues.quote: Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis).

issues.subcategory: gambling frequency measurement contradiction
issues.description: The manuscript first says gambling frequency will be assessed using a single item, then says an average across gambling behaviors will be taken. The supplemental materials show only a single item ('Gambled or placed bets at all'). If multiple behavior-specific items are not administered, an average across behaviors cannot be computed.
issues.quote: We will assess gambling frequency using a single item... To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.

issues.subcategory: oversampling gamblers biases gambling analyses
issues.description: The sports-wagering oversample means the gambling analyses will be dominated by people selected specifically for recent sports wagering. Sports bettors may differ from other gamblers in age, gender, religiosity, impulsivity, moral attitudes, and gambling severity. Without stratified or weighted analyses, results may not generalize to gambling broadly.
issues.quote: we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically.

issues.subcategory: missing clinical diagnostic controls
issues.description: The study aims to draw implications for diagnostic caveats in CSBD and addictive disorders but relies entirely on self-report symptom screens in a community sample. There are no clinician-administered diagnoses, impairment interviews, behavioral verification, or measures to distinguish moral distress from clinical impairment. This weakens diagnostic conclusions.
issues.quote: Interacting between moral disapproval and behavioral frequency will be tested... to establish whether moral incongruence is related to self-reported feelings of addiction

issues.subcategory: causal language from cross-sectional data
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly uses causal or directional language such as 'influences,' 'affecting,' and 'contributor' despite a cross-sectional observational design. Moral disapproval may be caused by perceived addiction, by consequences, by treatment exposure, or by third variables. Although limitations mention cross-sectionality, the hypotheses and implications still overstate causal inference.
issues.quote: we seek to establish whether moral incongruence... influences self-perceived feelings of addiction

issues.subcategory: unaddressed confounding
issues.description: The models adjust only for age, gender, and religiousness. Many plausible confounders could influence both moral disapproval and self-reported addiction symptoms, including political ideology, education, race/ethnicity, income, marital status, mental distress, impulsivity, substance availability/legal context, prior treatment, and social desirability. Omitted confounding threatens interpretation of the moral-incongruence effect.
issues.quote: In each case, we intend on including religiousness, age, and gender as covariates

issues.subcategory: gender coding underspecified and potentially exclusionary
issues.description: Gender is coded as binary in the interaction visualization and regression covariates, but the panel may include nonbinary or other gender responses. The plan does not state how gender categories beyond male/female will be handled or whether participants will be excluded or collapsed into 'not-male.' This affects reproducibility and inclusivity.
issues.quote: Interactions will be tested using this program with gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male), age, and overall religiousness included as covariates

issues.subcategory: religiousness as proxy for moral values
issues.description: The manuscript argues that moral incongruence in pornography is likely uniquely related to religious values but measures moral disapproval directly and includes religiousness as a covariate. Treating religiousness as both a conceptual source of moral incongruence and a covariate may remove theoretically meaningful variance or produce suppression effects. The theoretical role of religiousness is not clearly specified.
issues.quote: Taken together, these findings provide strong evidence for the argument that moral incongruence in the context of pornography use is likely uniquely related to religious values.

issues.subcategory: frequency measure lacks quantity/intensity
issues.description: Behavioral frequency is used as the behavioral component of moral incongruence, but frequency alone may poorly represent involvement or severity across domains. Alcohol frequency without quantity differs from heavy drinking; gambling frequency ignores money wagered/losses; nicotine frequency categories collapse amount and dependence; pornography frequency ignores duration. This threatens cross-domain comparability.
issues.quote: for the sake of the present study, we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed).

issues.subcategory: different time frames for predictors and outcomes
issues.description: Predictors and outcomes use inconsistent recall windows: past-year frequency, past-three-month ASSIST problem items, lifetime/past-three-month concern/control items, past-six-month BPS, and past-twelve-month PGSI. Interactions between past-year behavior and moral disapproval may not correspond temporally to outcomes, increasing measurement error and weakening causal/directional interpretation.
issues.quote: Beginning with the NIDA Quick Screen, we will assess past year frequency... Participants will respond to three frequency based questions... In the past three months... Participants will also respond to two questions... ever... In the last 6 months... Brief Pornography Screen

issues.subcategory: OLS for bounded ordinal/skewed outcomes without prespecified alternatives
issues.description: The outcomes are sums or averages of bounded ordinal items with expected zero inflation and skew, especially in community samples for illicit drugs, prescription misuse, gambling problems, and pornography problems. The plan mentions supplemental analyses if assumptions are violated but does not prespecify which models will be used. OLS may yield biased standard errors and inappropriate inference for sparse outcomes.
issues.quote: As a primary test of our key hypotheses, we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function in the stats package for R statistical software

issues.subcategory: unspecified supplemental analyses for assumption violations
issues.description: The analytic plan says alternative analyses will be conducted 'as appropriate' if regression assumptions are violated, but does not specify robust standard errors, transformations, ordinal models, zero-inflated models, generalized linear models, or decision thresholds. This leaves substantial researcher degrees of freedom in a registered report.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate.

issues.subcategory: incorrect claim about Holm-adjusted test statistics
issues.description: Holm adjustment changes p-value thresholds or adjusted p-values, not the test statistics themselves. The statement suggests confusion about multiple-comparison correction reporting. This is minor but indicates imprecise statistical reporting.
issues.quote: Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics using the psych package.

issues.subcategory: multiple testing not controlled for primary hypotheses
issues.description: The study proposes many moderation tests across substances and outcomes, plus equivalence tests and exploratory/fallback analyses, but no familywise or false discovery adjustment is specified for the primary regression tests. Given at least seven or eight interaction tests, false-positive risk is substantial, especially for claims that moral incongruence is unique to one domain.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest

issues.subcategory: uniqueness claim not directly tested
issues.description: The hypotheses test whether non-pornography interactions are statistically equivalent to zero, but uniqueness of pornography would require direct comparisons of interaction coefficients across domains with comparable measurement and uncertainty. Different outcomes, scales, distributions, reliabilities, and samples make absence/presence of significance or equivalence insufficient to establish a unique phenomenon.
issues.quote: should we find that moral incongruence—defined as the interaction between moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior—only predicts self-reported problematic use of pornography, then this work would provide strong evidence for the validity of the PPMI as a unique model

issues.subcategory: non-equivalent outcome measures across domains
issues.description: Pornography, gambling, and substances are assessed with different instruments, response scales, time windows, and item content. Cross-domain conclusions about whether moral incongruence is stronger or unique to pornography may reflect measurement differences rather than substantive differences.
issues.quote: Alcohol | Average of modified NIDA-ASSIST items... Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items Gambling Behavior | Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items

issues.subcategory: self-perceived addiction versus disorder symptoms conflated
issues.description: The manuscript alternates between self-reported feelings of addiction, problematic use, addiction symptoms, dysregulation, and disorder symptoms. These constructs are not interchangeable, especially for substances and gambling where diagnostic criteria exist. Conflation may lead to overinterpretation of self-report screen scores as disorder symptoms.
issues.quote: We expect to find that moral incongruence as it relates to gambling behaviors, will not predict self-reported levels of gambling disorder symptoms.

issues.subcategory: screening only users creates conditioning/collider concerns
issues.description: Problem-use items are administered only to participants reporting past-year use, and analyses appear to use subsets of users. Conditioning on use can alter associations between moral disapproval and problem symptoms because moral disapproval may predict abstention or lower frequency. This can introduce selection/collider bias and limits inference to users rather than the population.
issues.quote: Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use.

issues.subcategory: contradiction about administering key measures to all participants
issues.description: The methods first state that only users complete further problematic-use measures, but later state that key problematic-use and moral-disapproval measures will be administered to all participants regardless of engagement. These are incompatible. The analytic sample and missing-data structure are therefore unclear.
issues.quote: For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior. That is, we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample.

issues.subcategory: exclusion/inclusion criteria ambiguous
issues.description: It is unclear whether primary analyses include all participants, only past-year users, or different subsets depending on outcome. The text suggests both all-participant administration and user-only skip logic. Clear inclusion criteria are essential because moral incongruence hypotheses depend heavily on whether abstainers are included.
issues.quote: Therefore, for each analysis, we anticipate having slightly different subsets of the total sample.

issues.subcategory: power table sample sizes assume combined sample despite representativeness issue
issues.description: The effective Ns in Table 2 appear to apply prevalence percentages to the full N=4000, including the sports-betting oversample. For gambling, it combines 73% of the national sample with 100% of oversample, but for other behaviors assumes oversample prevalence equals population prevalence. If sports bettors differ in substance use or pornography prevalence, effective Ns and power estimates may be inaccurate.
issues.quote: Pornography Use | 60% | 2,400... Alcohol | 70% | 2800... Gambling | 73%  (national sample) 100%  (sports-betting oversample) | 3,325

issues.subcategory: Table 2 formatting corrupts reproducibility
issues.description: Table 2 contains repeated footnote text duplicated across table columns, making the table difficult to interpret and potentially obscuring values. This is a reporting problem for the power analysis, which is central to evaluating the registered report.
issues.quote: 1. All substance estimates based on the 2019-2020 National Survey on Drug Use and Health... | 1. All substance estimates based on the 2019-2020 National Survey on Drug Use and Health... | 1. All substance estimates based on the 2019-2020 National Survey on Drug Use and Health

issues.subcategory: missing details of YouGov matching
issues.description: The paper does not specify how matching will be conducted, what target distributions will be used, whether race/ethnicity, education, region, income, or political variables will be matched or weighted, and how panel recruitment probabilities are handled. 'Matched to U.S. representative norms' is insufficient for reproducibility.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms.

issues.subcategory: lack of blinding to study purpose/demand characteristics
issues.description: Participants answer moral disapproval and problem-use items about the same behaviors in close proximity. Without randomization of item order or procedures to reduce demand characteristics, respondents may infer that moral disapproval is relevant and answer problem items consistently with moral judgments. This is particularly concerning because all data are self-report.
issues.quote: Additionally, we will include a series of single-item moral disapproval questions that match previous measures of moral disapproval of pornography.

issues.subcategory: measure order not specified
issues.description: The manuscript does not specify the order of moral disapproval, frequency, and problem-use measures or whether item order is randomized. Order effects are plausible because moral framing may influence subsequent self-reported problems or vice versa.
issues.quote: Key measures described below are available in supplemental materials submitted with this Stage 1 Registered Report proposal.

issues.subcategory: pornography definition excludes partnered use in frequency item
issues.description: The frequency item assesses 'viewed pornography alone,' while the moral disapproval item refers to pornography use generally and the BPS asks about use of pornography generally. Participants who use pornography with partners may be misclassified as non-users or low-frequency users, weakening validity of the frequency predictor and interaction.
issues.quote: Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner)

issues.subcategory: gambling definition and item collapse heterogeneous activities
issues.description: A single global gambling frequency item collapses lotteries, casino gambling, sports betting, cards, fantasy sports, and online betting. These differ markedly in moral attitudes, risk, frequency, stakes, and addiction liability. A single moral disapproval item may not correspond to the specific gambling activities participants engage in.
issues.quote: Examples of these types of activities include: gambling in casinos or online, buying lottery tickets, playing fantasy sports for money, placing bets on esports, placing bets on traditional sporting events, playing cards for money, placing bets online.

issues.subcategory: substance categories too heterogeneous
issues.description: The categories 'illegal/illicit drugs' and 'prescription drugs for non-medical reasons' combine substances with different moral meanings, legal statuses, dependence potential, use patterns, and harms. This may obscure or distort moral incongruence effects and makes comparisons with pornography or gambling difficult.
issues.quote: Illegal/Illicit Drugs

issues.subcategory: alcohol binge item label error
issues.description: The male-specific alcohol item says 'more than 5 drinks' in the prompt but the table row label says 'More than four drinks.' This creates ambiguity in the actual administered item and could affect alcohol-use classification.
issues.quote: IF GENDER = MAN In the past year, how often have you had more than 5 drinks on one occasion?... More than four drinks (1)

issues.subcategory: no preregistration repository or Stage 1 acceptance details
issues.description: The manuscript is labeled a Registered Report and mentions a preregistered design but does not provide a registration URL, timestamp, analysis scripts, or explicit distinction between confirmatory and exploratory analyses beyond some contingencies. Registered-report transparency requires these details.
issues.quote: Although the proposed work has many strengths (nationally representative sample, pre-registered design, rigorous statistical evaluation of hypotheses)

issues.subcategory: industry-related funding conflict not analytically addressed
issues.description: The larger project is funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming, but the manuscript does not describe conflict-of-interest management, funder role, data access, or safeguards for analyses involving gambling. Given the gambling-industry-adjacent topic, transparency is important for credibility.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited in late March of 2022 as a part of a larger study of sports wagering behaviors in the American populace funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming.

issues.subcategory: misleading claim that CSBD is unique across all diagnostic manuals
issues.description: The manuscript asserts CSBD is the only recognized disorder in any diagnostic manual to include a caveat about moral distress. Even if true in a narrow sense, the claim is broad and not adequately qualified; many diagnoses include exclusions or cultural/contextual caveats. This overstatement motivates the uniqueness hypothesis and should be more carefully framed.
issues.quote: At present, CSBD is the only recognized disorder in any diagnostic manual to include such a caveat

issues.subcategory: ICD diagnostic caveat extrapolated from pornography to CSBD
issues.description: The study primarily tests pornography use, but CSBD encompasses broader sexual behavior. Evidence that moral incongruence predicts or does not predict pornography problems cannot fully justify claims about CSBD as a diagnostic category. The manuscript overextends pornography findings to sexual behavior and CSBD.
issues.quote: Demonstrating that moral incongruence appears to only be relevant in predicting feelings of dysregulation for sexual behaviors would corroborate the importance of CSBD being the only disorder to include a consideration about moral distress.

issues.subcategory: population sample used to infer clinical false positives
issues.description: The authors discuss implications for false-positive clinical diagnoses, but the sample is nonclinical and measures are self-report screens rather than diagnostic assessments. Population associations may not translate to treatment-seeking or diagnostically evaluated individuals.
issues.quote: there would be additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD.

issues.subcategory: moderation with centered ordinal predictors treated as interval
issues.description: The frequency predictors use coarse ordinal categories such as never, once/twice, monthly, weekly, daily, and more than daily. Treating these as equally spaced interval predictors in linear interactions assumes equal distance between categories, which is implausible and differs across behaviors. This can distort interaction estimates and simple slopes.
issues.quote: focal predictors (behavioral frequency measures) and moderators (moral disapproval questions) will be centered and their interaction term calculated.

issues.subcategory: standardization/centering ambiguity
issues.description: The plan says ASSIST items and religiousness will be standardized in SPSS, then says focal predictors and moderators will be centered, and later says key variables will be entered in raw form and their product computed. It is unclear whether interactions use raw, centered, or standardized variables. This affects β estimates and equivalence testing.
issues.quote: SPSS will be used to transform the above-described ASSIST items and measures of religiousness into standardized variables... focal predictors... and moderators... will be centered and their interaction term calculated... key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed.

issues.subcategory: no plan for interpreting interactions
issues.description: The authors plan to graph interactions but do not specify whether simple slopes, Johnson-Neyman intervals, regions of significance, or marginal effects will be reported, nor how interactions will be interpreted for bounded ordinal predictors. This limits reproducibility and interpretive rigor.
issues.quote: To visualize results, consistent with prior works on moral incongruence... we will make use of the Interactive Shiny application

issues.subcategory: moral incongruence not directly measured as discrepancy/distress
issues.description: The construct is defined as a misalignment between values and behavior, but the study operationalizes it statistically as a product term between moral disapproval and frequency. This does not directly measure subjective incongruence, distress about incongruence, or perceived value violation; high moral disapproval and high frequency may not necessarily mean the participant experiences incongruence.
issues.quote: moral incongruence (defined as the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior)

issues.subcategory: reverse causation not addressed in model
issues.description: People who experience addiction symptoms or consequences may increase moral disapproval of the behavior after problems emerge. The cross-sectional moderation model cannot distinguish moral disapproval amplifying perceived addiction from addiction symptoms leading to stronger moral judgments.
issues.quote: moral disapproval of pornography likely amplifies the links between pornography use and self-reported feelings of compulsivity or addiction.

issues.subcategory: no measurement invariance across domains or groups
issues.description: The study compares interactions across gender, substance categories, gambling, and pornography but does not assess whether scales function similarly across groups or domains. Differences in reliability, item difficulty, or response styles could masquerade as differences in moral incongruence effects.
issues.quote: Descriptive statistics for included measures, as well as measures of internal consistency for included scales (Cronbach’s alpha and Omega total), will be calculated

issues.subcategory: Cronbach alpha/omega for very short heterogeneous scales
issues.description: The modified ASSIST outcomes combine five heterogeneous indicators with different formats and time frames. Reporting alpha and omega may be psychometrically inappropriate unless unidimensionality is established. No factor-analytic plan is specified despite references to psychometrics in the bibliography.
issues.quote: Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest

issues.subcategory: no handling of legal-context variation
issues.description: Cannabis legality, gambling legality, and sports betting availability vary by U.S. state and may shape both moral disapproval and behavior frequency. State is available in panel data but not included in covariates or stratification. Ignoring legal context may confound moral wrongness with lawfulness/access.
issues.quote: given the heterogeneity of cannabis laws in the U.S. and the now-widespread, legal use of THC, we will add cannabis/THC related products

issues.subcategory: missing social desirability or stigma controls
issues.description: Self-reports of morally loaded behaviors and problems may be strongly affected by social desirability, shame, and stigma. The study’s central predictor is moral disapproval, which may correlate with response bias. No social-desirability or stigma measures are included, limiting interpretation.
issues.quote: The present work seeks to more fully understand the role that personal morality plays in affecting how people interpret their own potentially addictive behaviors.

issues.subcategory: unclear alpha level for equivalence and NHST
issues.description: The manuscript states α = .05 in power table notes but does not clearly specify whether equivalence tests use 90% CIs/two one-sided tests, Anderson-Hauck α, or 95% CIs for equivalence. Later it refers to confidence intervals falling within the equivalence region without specifying CI level. This ambiguity affects conclusions of equivalence.
issues.quote: Should the confidence interval for the observed standardized effect of the interaction... fall fully within our equivalence region

issues.subcategory: using self-reported 'feelings of addiction' for substances with established disorders
issues.description: For alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, prescription drugs, and illicit substances, the outcomes are modified screen averages rather than validated DSM/ICD substance-use-disorder criteria or diagnoses. Calling them substance use disorder symptoms is not justified by the measurement plan.
issues.quote: We expect to find that moral incongruence, as it relates to substance use, will also not predict self-reported symptoms of substance use disorders.

issues.subcategory: abstract says substances are 'recognized addictive disorders'
issues.description: The abstract and introduction describe alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, illicit substances, and prescription misuse as 'recognized addictive disorders,' but the study measures use categories and self-report problem items, not disorders. This mislabels the level of analysis and may overstate diagnostic relevance.
issues.quote: recognized addictive disorders such as gambling and substance use disorders (i.e., alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, illicit substances, and prescription drug misuse)

issues.subcategory: U.S.-only cultural context limits morality conclusions
issues.description: The study addresses broad theoretical claims about morality and addiction but samples only U.S. adults. Moral norms around pornography, gambling, alcohol, cannabis, and drugs vary widely across cultures and legal regimes. The limitations mention this but the introduction and implications often frame conclusions broadly.
issues.quote: we propose making use of an upcoming, nationally representative study of addictions in the U.S. population

issues.subcategory: unspecified primary pornography outcome
issues.description: Pornography is assessed with both the BPS and modified NIDA-ASSIST items, and gambling with PGSI and modified NIDA-ASSIST items. The plan does not clearly distinguish which outcome is primary for each hypothesis or how discrepant results will be handled. This creates multiple-outcome flexibility.
issues.quote: Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items Gambling Behavior | Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items

issues.subcategory: unclear confirmatory versus exploratory status of modified ASSIST behavior outcomes
issues.description: The manuscript says the validated BPS and PGSI will be used, but also includes modified NIDA-ASSIST outcomes for pornography and gambling and later bases contingency equivalence comparisons on the modified NIDA-ASSIST pornography outcome. The status of these analyses is unclear, allowing selective emphasis.
issues.quote: Specifically, we will use the lower limit of the 95% confidence interval around the obtained standardized estimate for the effect of the interaction of moral disapproval and pornography viewing frequency in predicting self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography using the modified NIDA-ASSIST items for pornography.

issues.subcategory: expected sample size for prescription misuse may be too low for interaction reliability
issues.description: The projected n = 140 for prescription drug misuse is very small for a six-predictor moderation model using skewed ordinal outcomes. Even if powered to detect a large pornography-like effect, estimates will be unstable with wide CIs and potentially sparse outcome categories. The planned fallback does not solve instability or precision limitations.
issues.quote: Even our smallest projected sample size (prescription drug misuse, at a prevalence of 3.5%, project n = 140) is more than sufficiently powered to detect such an effect (1 – β = .983).

issues.subcategory: no plan for rare-event/sparse-data problems
issues.description: Illicit drug and prescription misuse subgroups will be small and may have highly skewed problem scores, making linear interaction estimates unstable. The manuscript acknowledges power limitations but not sparse-cell diagnostics, minimum cell counts, or model convergence/robustness criteria.
issues.quote: in the case of illicit drug use... and prescription drug misuse... it is possible, if not probable, that our final sample sizes will fall below the minimum size required to detect effects that small

issues.subcategory: disapproval direct effect prediction contradicts uniqueness argument
issues.description: The authors predict positive direct effects of moral disapproval for gambling and substances but no interactions. Yet if moral disapproval predicts self-reported problems across domains, this already challenges the claim that morality is uniquely relevant to sexual behavior, depending on the theoretical definition. The conceptual distinction between direct moral disapproval effects and moral incongruence is not adequately integrated into the diagnostic implication.
issues.quote: Specifically, we do expect moral disapproval of substances among substance users to positively predict self-reported problems

issues.subcategory: moral wrongness may reflect objective harm rather than personal incongruence
issues.description: For substances such as illicit drugs, prescription misuse, tobacco, and heavy alcohol use, moral wrongness may be based on perceived harm to self/others, legality, or public health rather than personal values conflicting with one's own behavior. The single item cannot distinguish these sources, weakening construct validity for moral incongruence.
issues.quote: I believe that using ________ is morally wrong

issues.subcategory: no data/code availability plan
issues.description: A registered report should specify whether deidentified data, code, survey materials, and analysis scripts will be made available, especially because YouGov panel data and proprietary procedures may restrict sharing. The manuscript does not include a reproducibility plan.
issues.quote: Data will be provided by YouGov in SPSS format.

issues.subcategory: panel data covariates may be outdated
issues.description: Age, gender, and religiousness are taken from YouGov panel data rather than assessed in the survey. Some variables, especially religiousness and gender identity, may change or be missing/outdated. The manuscript does not report when panel data were collected or how stale covariate data will be handled.
issues.quote: Age, gender, and religiousness will be assessed using panel data provided by YouGov (i.e., not as a part of our survey).

issues.subcategory: duplicated title and Registered Report heading
issues.description: The title and Registered Report heading appear twice, suggesting manuscript assembly issues. While not directly threatening validity, it signals potential version-control/reporting problems also reflected in table and scale inconsistencies.
issues.quote:
Moral Incongruence and Addiction:

A Registered Report

... Moral Incongruence and Addiction:

A Registered Report

issues.subcategory: no ethical/IRB and consent details
issues.description: The study surveys sensitive sexual behavior, gambling, and drug use, yet the methods do not describe IRB approval, informed consent, participant compensation, confidentiality protections, or resources for distress/problem gambling/substance use. These details are important for evaluating ethical conduct and response validity.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited in late March of 2022 as a part of a larger study of sports wagering behaviors

issues.subcategory: independence assumption not matched to panel and matched sample design
issues.description: The plan says independence of residuals will be tested, but survey panel data with matching/weights may violate simple independence through household, geographic, or recruitment-cluster effects. The plan does not include cluster-robust or survey-weighted variance estimation.
issues.quote: Prior to our primary analyses, assumptions of regression (i.e., linearity, independence of residuals, homoscedasticity of residuals, normality of residuals) will be tested

issues.subcategory: ASSIST alcohol modification weakens validated hazardous-use screening
issues.description: The NIDA Quick Screen alcohol item is designed around heavy episodic drinking thresholds, but the primary frequency predictor is changed to any alcohol use. This may make casual low-risk drinking appear frequent and reduce alignment with addiction/problem severity. It also weakens comparability to validated ASSIST scoring.
issues.quote: Although we will include these response options, for the sake of the present study, we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed).

issues.subcategory: Table 1 excludes alcohol heavy-drinking item
issues.description: The supplemental materials include gender-specific heavy drinking items, but the analytic plan says alcohol frequency will be general alcohol use. It is unclear whether heavy drinking items will be analyzed, used in scoring, or ignored, creating ambiguity in alcohol operationalization.
issues.quote:
IF GENDER = WOMAN

In the past year, how often have you had more than 4 drinks on one occasion?

issues.subcategory: covariate set underjustified and fixed despite available variables
issues.description: The manuscript lists many available demographic and political variables but only includes age, gender, and religiousness. The selection is only partly justified from pornography literature and may not be appropriate for substances/gambling. Not specifying sensitivity analyses with available confounders increases risk of omitted-variable bias and selective modeling.
issues.quote:
Supplemental Materials

YouGov Panel Data Included

Birth Year

Gender

Race

Education... Ideology... Religious affiliation

issues.subcategory: confirmation framed as support for ICD-11 caveat without diagnostic test
issues.description: The study’s logic assumes that if moral incongruence interactions are unique to pornography self-reports, this supports ICD-11’s moral distress caveat. But ICD-11 caveat concerns differential diagnosis and sufficiency of distress, not whether a cross-sectional interaction predicts self-reported symptoms. The inference from statistical moderation to diagnostic validity is conceptually indirect.
issues.quote: should hypotheses be confirmed, there would be additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD.

issues.subcategory: no specification of exclusion for underage respondents
issues.description: The sample is described as American adults, but the pornography and gambling measures may require age restrictions depending on platform and state. The manuscript does not specify age minimum, verification, or handling of respondents under 21 for gambling/sports betting context.
issues.quote: the target sample size will be 2,500 American adults

issues.subcategory: moral disapproval of behavior may not equal disapproval of one's own behavior
issues.description: The theoretical model concerns distress about one's own behavior, but the measure asks whether the behavior is morally wrong in general. People may disapprove generally but excuse their own use, or vice versa. This mismatch can weaken or bias measurement of personal moral incongruence.
issues.quote: I believe that pornography use is morally wrong

issues.subcategory: using standardized beta for equivalence across different outcome reliabilities
issues.description: The equivalence tests rely on standardized regression coefficients across different outcomes and predictors. Standardized betas vary with sample distributions, outcome variance, reliability, and oversampling, so they are not necessarily comparable across behaviors. Using a pornography-derived β SESOI for substances/gambling may be misleading.
issues.quote: we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above

issues.subcategory: no attention to legal/age eligibility for sports wagering oversample
issues.description: Sports wagering legality varies by state and age. The oversample criterion is 'recent history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically,' but the recruitment method, legality, and verification are not described. This may affect sample composition and reporting accuracy.
issues.quote: an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically

issues.subcategory: PGSI scoring changed from sum to average
issues.description: The standard PGSI is typically summed and interpreted with established risk categories. The manuscript says responses will be averaged, and the supplemental response coding is nonstandard. This may preclude use of validated cutoffs and comparability with prior research.
issues.quote: Responses will be averaged.

issues.subcategory: BPS scoring changed from validated response values
issues.description: The Brief Pornography Screen is described with one response scale in the text and another in the supplement. If nonstandard scoring is used, validation evidence and cutoffs may not apply. This matters because BPS is the primary validated pornography outcome.
issues.quote: Brief Pornography Screen... | Never (0) | Occasionally (2) | Very Often (4)

issues.subcategory: unclear handling of 'not applicable' for nonusers
issues.description: If nonusers receive problem-use measures, items such as urges, problems, and failed control may be nonsensical; if they are skipped, outcomes are missing by design. The plan does not specify whether nonusers receive zeros, are excluded, or are coded missing. Each choice changes the estimand.
issues.quote: only participants who report viewing pornography at least once in the past 12 months... will complete the remaining items described below

issues.subcategory: third-variable psychopathology not measured
issues.description: General distress, anxiety, depression, OCD symptoms, impulsivity, and shame proneness could influence both moral disapproval and self-perceived addiction. The study aims to infer that morality shapes interpretation of addiction but does not adjust for these important psychological confounds.
issues.quote: The primary focus of this project is to assess... how those behaviors relate to a wide variety of other behavioral addiction symptoms, substance use behaviors, and general mental well-being.

issues.subcategory: alcohol item says men five or more but supplemental says more than 5
issues.description: The text describes the NIDA threshold as five or more drinks for men, but the supplemental item asks more than 5 drinks, which excludes exactly five drinks. This affects comparability with the original NIDA Quick Screen and sex-specific hazardous drinking criteria.
issues.quote: asks men to report alcohol frequency in terms of how many days they have consumed five or more drinks in a day

issues.subcategory: linearity assumption implausible for frequency categories
issues.description: The proposed linear models assume the relation between frequency categories and symptom scores is linear. For addictive behaviors, risk may increase nonlinearly or threshold-like. No plan for polynomial, dummy-coded, or ordinal contrast sensitivity analyses is specified.
issues.quote: assumptions of regression (i.e., linearity... ) will be tested

issues.subcategory: vague robustness criterion based on sign and significance
issues.description: The plan defines robustness as sign and significance remaining the same across analytic techniques. This is an inadequate and potentially misleading criterion, especially for equivalence hypotheses and effect-size interpretation. It also leaves unspecified which result will be considered primary if effect sizes differ meaningfully but significance does not.
issues.quote: Should results of moderation analyses remain robust (i.e., sign and significance of interaction effects remain the same across analytic techniques), we will present OLS results

issues.subcategory: behavioral addiction terminology overextended
issues.description: The manuscript includes substances, gambling, pornography, and sometimes internet/gaming under broad 'addiction' language, but addiction status and diagnostic recognition vary substantially. This imprecision can obscure whether the study is about perceived addiction, compulsivity, moralized behavior, or recognized disorders.
issues.quote: moral disapproval is likely present in the full spectrum of addictions, both substance and behavioral

issues.subcategory: no sample-size stopping rule beyond target
issues.description: The target sample is stated, but the manuscript does not specify stopping rules, replacement procedures if quotas are not met, whether oversampling continues until complete cases are achieved, or how deviations from target N will be handled.
issues.quote: the target sample size will be 2,500 American adults... recruit an additional 1,500 adults

issues.subcategory: past-year use eligibility with past-three-month symptoms excludes remitted cases inconsistently
issues.description: Participants with past-year use but no past-three-month use may answer ASSIST symptom items about the past three months with zeros, while lifetime failed-control items may still be positive. This mixes current and historical problems in a single outcome and may distort associations with current frequency.
issues.quote: Beginning with the NIDA Quick Screen, we will assess past year frequency... To assess problematic or potentially addictive use... In the past three months... Has a friend or relative or anyone else ever expressed concern... Have you ever tried and failed

issues.subcategory: interaction interpretation with main effects and covariates not fully specified
issues.description: The hypotheses refer to direct effects of moral disapproval 'among users' while also including frequency and interaction. In an interaction model, the main effect of moral disapproval is conditional on the centered value of frequency. The manuscript does not specify the centering point or interpret this conditional effect correctly.
issues.quote: We expect to find that the simple, direct effect of moral disapproval of pornography on self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography will be significant and positive, even when use frequency, religiousness, gender, and age are included as covariates in a regression model.

issues.subcategory: hypothesis numbering referenced but not shown
issues.description: The analytic plan references hypotheses 2b and 3b, but the hypotheses are not numbered in the manuscript as presented. This creates ambiguity about which exact hypotheses are supported by equivalence tests.
issues.quote: thereby supporting hypotheses 2b and 3b, listed above.
